Not even the workingman would suffer more from the success of the democratic party than would the business men of the country. That party opposes the principle of protection, and favors what the London Times says is something that is not protection. The southern leaders, one and all, oppose the principle of protection on constitutional grounds, and northern democrats are now, as they have ever been, under the absolute domination of the south. It was on the ground that a protective tariff was unconstitutional that South Carolina passed her notification laws and drew from Andrew Jackson his grand message—a message hateful now to southerners and their allies. It is therefore the south against the north upon a question that first led to rebellion and secession.

But who will, or who can, authoritatively deny this power? There is one tribunal, and only one, that can authoritatively deny it—the Supreme Court of the United States—and there is one tribunal that might by possibility come into existence that would deny it, and that is a supreme court composed of men a majority of whom would be appointed by a democratic president. Two men, Fuller and Lamar, have been chosen by Mr. Cleveland, men with no other recommendation than their intense and extreme advocacy of interchangeable doctrines. No one who judges from experience can doubt that bench composed of such men would carry into effect what for so many years was proclaimed in democratic platforms as that time-honored principle of the democratic party. THE BEAUTIFUL SCIENCE.


FRIENDS OF THE SCIENCE. In response TO many
pleasant letters requesting me to write something
more on the subject of botany, I will say that I
perceive such amount of interest in this
beautiful science, and I will cheerfully do what I
can to promote the pleasure of the friends in its
pursuit. Several have expressed wish to
exchange plants with me—if they only knew how to
prepare the specimens. The following hints it is
hoped, will be of use to those in need of such in-
sistance.


First, a few words in regard to collecting speci-
mens for Science herbarium. Of botanical specimens—a more
scientific term—should either be flower or in
fruit, many herbaceous plants presenting both at
the same time. The entire plant should be taken,
if not too large, including the root, at least a
portion of it. In the case of shrubs, trees or large
plants enough should be taken TO show the general
character and habit of growth. If we are not pro-
vided with a collecting can—which is much the
best article to use for this purpose—we shall want
a covered basket, or some other convenient recep-
tacle, for bringing home the specimens which are
likely to become wilted and unfit for use if carried
in the hand. A press-book, which is simply
portfolio filled with sheets of drying paper,
will be found exceedingly useful for receiving
delicate specimens, which will be pre-
served in best shape if put under moderate
pressure soon they are taken. A knife is a
necessity, and a pair of scissors quite handy. With
this equipment one may do very well. It is not
advisable to load ourselves with all the various
tools and uses which are often recommended.


In placing the specimens IN press should
be done carefully. It may be in their natural
state, as a dried specimen on a drying paper be-
tween two flat sheets preferred by some—and
if these dried sheets they must be used until
they are thoroughly dried. The paper
used for this purpose should be thin blotting
paper; if this is not to be had, however, we can do fairly
well with old newspapers cut IN sheets OF con-
stantly glazed, in that case it would not readily absorb
the moisture from the specimens and they would
not keep good color in drying out.


In addition to blotting drying paper, the her-
balists use a considerable number of papers
which are made of blotting paper, usually cut IN sheets
about 8 by 10 inches in size, and stitched together
along the edges eight to ten thicknesses of paper
being used for each sheet. We shall need a large
supply of these if we intend to put many specimens
in the press at one time.


For applying the pressure nothing is better than
the usual botanist's press, properly constructed.
A good substitute may be provided
by making a couple of press boards the size of the
papers—say 10 inches—for which the board used
should be stout enough to support the weights ap-
plied to produce the needful pressure.


Suppose that we have collected a num-
ber of specimens, and have apparatus already
for putting them to press; spread out a dryer,
upon which we place one of our specimens ar-
ranged on its drying paper, and lay over it another
dryer; then another specimen, another dryer and
so alternately until specimens are all in a
place. Will dryer at the top. Then we put the
whole pile in press, under moderate weight at
first and allow them to remain for six or
eight hours, when the dryers will be more
or less capable of absorbing moisture from the
specimens; they should then be re-
moved and replaced with a set of dry ones. In
connecting this change, we should be care-
ful not to disturb the specimens as they lie in the
drying leaves and we should be equally cautious
in transferring to the press the sheets containing
frail specimens, which have been brought home in
the press-book. After changing the driers we in-
crease the pressure by turning the screws of our
press, or putting on more weight, if the case may be.


The driers should be changed every day for the
first four days; after that once in two days until
the specimens are perfectly dry. This will require
more or less time in drying and some not so
long. We will guide you in this matter and
also in regard to the amount of pressure to be ap-
plied. On this point only general directions can
be given but it may be stated that ordinary spec-
imens will bear from 90 to 100 pounds; it is best
not to put very delicate specimens to press with
coarser kinds, lest they are likely to be injured by
great pressure. If we have a large number of
specimens to press shall find it necessary to
put on more weight than when we have but a few.


Specimens collected should be put in press as
soon as possible; they should be fresh and perfect
and dry. This does not apply to mosses, lichens and
algae, which may also be preserved in either moist
or dry state for a long time, and placed in the
press at any convenient opportunity. Mosses and
lichens are the better for being pressed when quite
damp and algae must be laid upon card in water
to preserve them in form. As
these curious plants require a special mode of
treatment, we need not consider them at this time.


The most essential point is to change the driers
at least often every other day; and if this is
not done, ever day until the specimens are well dried.

There were only five houses on the west side of the river, three frame and two of logs, opposite the present site of the Star Mills. There were no bridges, but the material for foot bridge was piled up near where Bridge-st. bridge now is, ready to be put across when the high water went down. There was ferry boat running across below the islands, upon one of which the THE-SEA-HERALD office now stands, and teams forded the river at this point when the water was not too high. The ferry landing was up the stream few rods, where the foundry now is, at the foot of Huron-st. There was a wing dam and a race, which discharged its waters back into the East channel at this point. This aspect of the monarch is strikingly brought out in the letter addressed by Frederick III to his Prime Minister.

Whosoever ignores the hidden meaning embodied in the document does not fully appreciate the virtue and force inherent in a character like that of Frederick III. Monarchs in such an exalted position who have inherited through a long line of ancestors both government and power in such a vast country as Germany and among men proud like Germans cannot think much less act, with the independence of those who have shaped their own fortunes, who have risen by their own eloquence, by their good star or by their merits, to high places in public favor. Frederick is an emperor, not a tribune, and yet, nevertheless, in his letters and in his recent proclamations, are found ideas and sentences stamped with the sentiments of a tribune.

Four principal features characterize the reign of Frederick, father, and the policy of the Chancellor. They are the anti-Catholic and anti-Semitic movement, state socialism, Caesarism and militarism. He tells the author of the May laws, the man who enthusiastically protected the old Catholics while he attempted to convert the orthodox Catholics of Germany into a semi-Protestant church; he tells the disciples of ex-Court Preacher Stocker, at the head of the anti-Semitic movement; he tells the advocates of scientific and religious socialism supported by the forces and powers of the state—Frederick tells them all that he far prefers to all these tyrannical and arbitrary sophisms the liberties and rights of our human conscience.

He faces that most eminent statesman who has devoted his whole political life, while holding the post of Chancellor, to the doctrines of state socialism, and reminds him that he cannot assent to the cabalistic formulas of this social alchemy, and that he believes it to be indispensable to return to the observance and accomplishment of all the great principles of political economy. He declares to those who have always shown more regard for personal power than for the constitution, identifying and confusing it with their notion of the state, that it is absolutely necessary to accept the cooperation of the nation and to respect its laws, because, above all other considerations, stand the rights of the German nation.

He admits that wicked military glory does not tempt nor seduce him, and dares to make this frank confession in that veritable camp called Germany, kept on such an offensive and defensive footing, that one might think Europe still lived in times of universal warfare; in that camp where the only mouths that open are those of cannon, the only flashes that light the air are the glintings of bayonets, and where everything is crowned with the peaked helmet of Mars.

To all this you add a very bitter criticism of the legislative mania of Bismarck, who would interfere with everything and regulate everything according to his own way of thinking. We may truly assert that never has a reign opened with such an absolute contrast with the proceeding one—that which exists between the reign of Frederick III and that of his great father, the modern William the Conqueror.

I have followed with great attention all Frederick's words and all his acts, and am able to say that I can never forget the delightful speech he made some years ago before the learned professors of Heidelberg University on the occasion of an academical centenary. storm last week in the State of Vera Cruz
wrought much damage along the line of the
Mexican Veracruz railway. The greatest
injury to the railway line was in the lar-

and more delic ols coffee is made by

ground coffee than by boiling the coffes
itself, as unfortunately is yet so often
done. The boiling water that is poured
over the coffee ceases TO boil the instant
it leaves the kettle in which it was boiled.

what cooled on the way to the coffee pot,
and by further contact with other bodies
the temperature is still further lowered
until it is evident that the temperature
in the coffee pot is several degrees be-
low the boiling point. The coffee is con-
sequently not made with boiling but with
warm water.

in Ireland.

KILRUSH, April 8th.—On SATURDAY night some policemen, who were trying to prevent the erection of a platform for a meeting announced to be held to-day, were pelted with stones by mob, and were compelled to charge the crowd. Many civilians were badly injured.

Mr. Tanner, member of Parliament, held meeting outside of Macroon at 5 o'clock this morning. He there burned a copy of the Government proclamation. At 2 P.M., the advertised hour, he attempted to hold another meeting, when the police removed him from the grounds and there was only slight excitement.

About 5000 persons belonging to various branches of the League assembled at 2:30 P.M. There was a large contingent on horseback. The police, led by the magistrates, charged through the crowd, injuring many. A number of triumphal arches were torn down. Father Glynn was protected by policemen with rifles.

CHARGE WITH BAYONETS.
A farmer felled one policeman with stick. A riot being imminent, the Berkshire Regiment, with fixed bayonets, charged the crowd and many persons were badly wounded.

Order was restored, and the crowd appealed to by priests and Messrs. Redmond, O'Reilly and other members of Parliament, who advised the multitude to disperse.

SERIOUS TROUBLE AT ENNIS
ENNIS, April 8th.—Messrs. Davitt, O'Connor, Rev. Mr. Cory and other League leaders left Ennis this afternoon and drove ten miles into the country, followed by eighty Hussars under Colonel Turner, and by preconcerted arrangement Mr. Condor, J.T., remained in town to hold the proposed meeting in an unoccupied store. This programme leaked out, and a cordon of soldiers were placed around the building. The doors had been barricaded, but soon gave way to sledge-hammers in the hands of the police. This aroused a desperate resistance on the part of the people present, and many were injured. Fifty persons were arrested, among them Dunleavy, editor of the Clare Independent.

SIMILAR PROCEEDINGS AT LOUGHREA
LOUGHREA, April 8th.—O'Brien held his meeting to-day. While the police were dispersing the people he spoke ten minutes. He called the police towards for not arresting him, instead of ill-treating the people.

Reaching the platform out of town, followed by 1000 people, he was met by an imposing force of police and military. He addressed the people to that, and addressed the magistrate to the following effect: "I wish to hold meeting to tell the people the truth about English rule in Ireland but no meeting will be held if it has been resolved to disperse the people forcibly."

O'Brien then said that if force was to be used, to use it on him, and not on the people. The crowd advanced toward the platform, and the police immediately attacked them, knocking down those who resisted.

OTHER MEETINGS DISPERSED.
KANTURK, April 8th.—Several hundred men, with National League cards displayed on their caps, paraded here to-day. In accordance with the announcement, Messrs. Healy and Flynn attempted to address the crowd of people that had assembled in town. They failed, as the crowd was immediately dispersed by the police.

The proposed League meeting at Ramsgrange was postponed for a week on account of the presence of formidable police force.

Rehabilitation of the Congregational

The Congregational church was re-dedicated on Sunday morning and the evening exercises were given over to what, in a social sense, would be called "house warming." Every pew was full in the morning and in the evening the pews and the sides of the main auditorium were jammed—indeed from gallery to gallery so scant was the standing room that several hundred were turned away.

The church choir, led by Mr. Harrison, never was so large, nor sang so well. The half dome and circular sounding board threw the entire volume of music from both choir and organ out into the church, and the effect was more clearly marked than ever before. The choir has shown great improvement in the past, and the improvement in the future, now that all have reached a tarry standing point, cannot fail to be noticeable.

The service opened with prayer by Mr. Whittlesey who read appropriate scripture selections. The sacerdotal prayer was a fine effort. Following Mr. Whittlesey, Mr. Day delivered the dedication sermon with even more than his usual force and eloquence. His theme, "THE real Glory Of the House Of God," was very ably handled, and abounded in logical truths and beautiful sentiments. The principal, or leading thoughts of his discourse were "There may be glory in the house of worship, glory of architecture and of adornment. There may be glory of adaptation. There may be glory in its expression of an Offering to God. But the highest glory of the House of God, is in the faith which it expresses in Christ, the power which it affords for Christ, and the place which it proffers for the presence of Christ."

The regular Sunday school exercises gave way to special service. Short addresses were made by the pastor, Mr. Whittlesey and others. A quartette, composed of Mrs. Blanchard, the Misses McNear, Miss DeLeagneau and Mr. Harrison, sang an appropriate number, which was very well received. A solo, by Ralph Sapp, was excellently rendered.

Dr. Fredericks, Mr. Holmes, Mr. McKay and Mr. Whittlesey, were on the rostrum with Mr. Day in the evening. Mr. Day made the opening address, and acted as master of ceremonies during the remainder of the evening, which was taken up with addresses by Mr. Holmes and Dr. Fredericks, and prayer by Mr. McKay; the service closing with the pronunciation of the benediction by Mr. Whittlesey. The music as in the morning service, was grand.

There are churches in the State whose interiors have cost a great deal more than that of the Congregational church, but it is doubted whether there is a church even in Chicago whose decorations, painting, upholstery and carpeting, equals in beauty or harmony, the interior of this edifice. The paint and fresco work has already been discussed in these columns, but little if any of the effect then produced is present now. The carpet, a fine ingrain, perfectly blending with the general tone of the upholstery, and the splendid new shade of lowered damask, imported especially for the purpose, changes the entire appearance of the entire interior. Each tint, whether of carpet, woodwork, upholstery or fresco, is in perfect harmony with the other. The rail of the east chair gallery, the rostrum chairs, and the pulpit are upholstered in elegant plush.

The heating apparatus, placed in by Mr. Gage, the famous furnace manufacturer, is as nearly perfect as could be desired. It stands upon brick piers, and instead of receiving its draft from the outside, as is usual with most furnaces, receives the cold air of the rooms underneath, heats it and sends it up through the huge registers placed side by side at the extreme west end of the auditorium. This rarefied air, pushing upwards and outward, sends the cold air of the room down into the rooms below through the large registers, and the circulating draft thus produced heats both lower and upper floor quickly and evenly.

Some few improvements are yet to be made, but there is little room for them.

WASHINGTON, May 26—The house passed yesterday in discussing unimportant amendments to the legislative, executive and judicial appropriation bill.

Private business was set aside, and the house in committee of the whole resumed consideration of the legislative, executive and judicial appropriation bill. The bill was read by paragraphs for amendment.

Mr. J. D. Taylor, of Ohio, offered an amendment increasing the salary of the chaplain of the house from 5000 to 6200, which created some discussion of a bantering character relative to the amount of prayer necessary for the well being of Democratic house. The amendment was rejected.

Several hours of dreary discussion on trivial amendments ensued.

Mr. Cobb, of Alabama, opposed the entire appropriation for the botanical garden. He said that when he first came to congress he had said to an old member that he would vote to abolish the garden. This member, an economy and reform Democrat too, told him that if he did he would be a "d—d fool." (Laughter.) He had then asked what was the use of it, and the reply was that one could procure flowers there. His informant could not tell where the flowers went, but knew that they did not go to the members' wives. (Laughter.)

social and commercial Standing.

has aroused great deal of indignation
among the whisky men, who are leaders in
business circles and regard themselves
quite as good Christians as anybody else.

be followed up by other churches, and in
that event the whisky men will very likely
establish church of their own.

The first concern of all good government is the virtue and sobriety of the people and the purity of the home. The Republican party cordially sympathizes with all wise and well directed efforts for the promotion of temperance and morality. Republican Platform, 1888.

Responding heartily to these noble sentiments and other enunciations of political truth concerning social, economic and moral questions contained in the comprehensive declarations of the NATIONAL REPUBLICAN PLATFORM, adopted by the recent convention at Chicago, we send greeting to the women of the United States, and ask them to make utterance of their devotion to home and country by giving active support to the Republican party in the pending campaign. We who send you this call do not claim pre-eminent devotion to home and country. We know that everywhere in our land are patriotic women; they love the flag, they waved it in holiday splendor under the blue sky of national prosperity; they revered it when its brightness was dimmed by the smoke of war. It is precious, the blood of kindred, sacred as the shroud of beloved dead, to all who believe that the flag is worth all it costs—to all loyal women this address comes.

The Republican party is not a sectional, it is a national party. In its ranks are wounded veterans of the Union army, and soldiers of the late Confederacy, and emancipated Slaves; the party knows no east, no west, no north, no south. Eastern culture and WESTERN ENTERPRISE have nurtured a Conservative radicalism as contiguous and continuous as is the transcontinental railway system which the Republican policy of internal improvements made possible.

Across the Bloody Chasm, a part of our heroic past, are the clasped hands of growing industries, sensitive and responsive with neap of trade. Steam and smoke and fame from furnace, factory and mill are the clouds by day and the fire by night, renewing the Republican principles, and guiding the country out from the wilderness of sectionalism into the promised land of perfectly restored nationalism.

In the ranks of the Republican party are found many citizens of foreign birth. In America they are Americans; they do not forget the mother country nor the fatherland, but here they are loyal to the stars and stripes; their loyalty was tested even to the shedding of blood in war; with whatever makes for good citizenship they welcome in the party; their rights under the flag command respect.

The achievements of this great PARTY have made luminous this country's history. Under God's blessing it rescued the imperiled nation, saved the Government our fathers gave us, and maintained the institutions which assure to American women the exalted position they now enjoy. The Republican party has always been the party of protection to the citizen, protection to the negro, protection to the ballot box, protection to the wage-earner, protection to the wage-layer, and now in line with past professions and performances it declares for protection for the "home." Can American women fail to respond?

This party is not a squad of untrained, untrained recruits, reckless to attempt and helpless to secure political defence; it is not a troop of detached soldiery on picket duty: it is THE REGULAR ARMY of AMERICAN PROGRESS; it was raised from the lifeblood of the people; its ranks are kept full by the farm, the shop, the school, the mill; it is sworn to champion at the command of the sovereign people.

Whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report, in Government.

American women, this is the party to whose service we call you. What position will you take and hold during the month of the coming campaign? Do you realize the moral side, the heart-side of the economic questions which are being discussed in the campaign? Do you remember that when labor is degraded, woman is degraded. The shop girl, the factory operative, the sewing woman, indeed every working woman whether she toil in home, of shop, or school, is interested in the maintenance of American standard of values in labor, and its return to the home. In November next, twelve million of voters will go to the polls and determine who shall receive the highest honor in the gift of the American people. Is this anything to you? Does it make ANY difference to you who this man is, and for what school of principles he stands?

Would not the choice of BENJAMIN HARRISON AND LEVI P. MORTON, as chief executives of this great nation, tend to establish popular standard of private morals and public service which any mother might present to the aspiration of her son? Do not their lives illustrate that purity in personal character is consonant with the highest worldly success? That the dealings in the heart of trade, the court of justice, the legislative chamber, or the camp of war need never have to blush in the home? Is it not vital to the character of the people's chief representatives?

Young women of the nation have too long to pay to that established order of things which we call Christian civilization: Do you realize that Republican Institutions are the material organism through which this spirit of civilization breathes? Will you not in thankful appreciation of the inheritance into which YOU have entered, pledge humble fealty to the Republican party, whose standard bearer wears the white flower of chastity and life?

Beyond the immediate demands of the present campaign lies the broad field of political duties. Women are equally concerned with men in the seed time and the harvest gathered there. KEEPERS OF THE NATION'S HOMES, educators of the Nation's children, sharers in its industries, and guardians of its truths, will YOU not also give your best brain and heart to the study of the principles of government and their application in practical politics? This civic ing shall not impoverish, its withholding has lost the heart of which can women.

The State is not less a divine institution than is the family where your throne is, the church where you and your children worship God and study His laws. Under our system of Government the state is that great temple which the people are forever building and rebuilding. If they build well the structure shall endure and safely protect our sacred interests from vandals without and from traitors within. With her are Lizzie Annandale, fine contralto, widely and well known; the new and successful young singer, Mira Bertini; the Spanish second tenor, Michelena, who has won high praise for his vocal power and management; Pruette, baritone; Broderick, the basso, long and well known here, and Walter Allen, one of the best singing comedians on the stage. Carl Martens, who was here the last opera season, still is director of the company. The sale of seats opens on Monday at $1.40 and 50 cents, and $1.80 for reserved seats.

After the snow blockade was lifted sixty nine bags of mail were delivered at Kimball.


The railroad company has woodpile of 700 cords at Nermillion and wants to double it.


It is thought that the Sioux Indian reservation will be opened for settlement in a few weeks.


The business men of Grand Forks decided last Tuesday to build a creamery to cost 5000.


Sioux Falls has started a subscription for the benefit of the Reading, Pennsylvania, strikers.


There was no one frozen to death in Sully county during the storm, but many report a close call.


The Mitchell Republican says but one life was lost in Dawson county in the blizzard of January.


Bismarck people are encouraged to believe that the Illinois Central will build to their city this year.


Mrs. Carl Sail, living near Zen, gave birth to twins Tuesday, this making the second pair within a year.


The Y.A.R. are preparing for a grand campfire at De Smet on Washington's birthday, February.


The Press says: It is evident that the crop of Pierre babies harvested during the coming year, will be the largest ever known.


About $1,000 of floating indebtedness of Pennington county has been paid in the last six months, having about $4,000 outstanding.


The commissioners of Brown county have awarded the county printing to the new democratic paper recently established in that county.


Two local pugilists fought seven rounds at Spencer last week. The fight, which took place in a wheat bin, in order to exclude police, was decided a draw.


The Washington Springs Republican says, that cattle are finding good grazing on the prairies of Jerauld county, and fresh, green grass is from one to three inches long.


Officer Paddock left Huron on Monday for Briton, having in custody W. X. Gettuan also of Briton, a knight of the green cloth who is charged with having been too familiar with another man's wife.


The family of John Quinn, twelve in number, living near Bridgewater, were all nearly suffocated last night by coal gas, which escaped from a stove. Medical assistance was promptly summoned, and they are recovering.


The Black Hills soldiers and sailors association was organized on the 13th ult. at Sturgis. Nineteen states were represented in the organization, with an enrolment of 100 members.


The court house at Sioux Falls is now without telephone connection. The commissioners would not pay for it and the sheriff can no longer.


Watertown now has one of the handsomes and best appointed post offices in the territory, a change having been made from the old building on Oak street to the large, commodious bank building of the Dakota Loan and Trust COMPANY on Kemp avenue.


A school teacher in Buffalo county, whose wife was one of his pupils, had occasion to punish her one day. The next day the school house door bore this inscription: "School closed for one week owing to the illness of the school teacher."


Three prisoners at Mitchell tackled the turnkey Monday night and escaped.

The New York Herald seems to be responsible for the facts in the following editorial clipped from The Pioneer:


The New York Herald of Wednesday devotes column and half to discussion of the present condition of things under the Brooks law in Philadelphia. The statements contained in the article confirm the soundness of the position that Prohibitionists have maintained with regard to what is popularly known as high license. There are 800 breweries in Philadelphia, and The Herald says: "The brewers are tickled to death over the unforeseen results brought about by this high license law." This is owing to the fact that their business has increased 30 per cent. since the Brooks law went into operation. The explanation of this lies in the fact that the trade in bottled beer has quadrupled since June 1.


In an interview with Mr. Bergner, of the Bergner and Engel Brewing company, one of the largest concerns in the city, making 10 per cent. of all the beer there, that experienced maltster says the law is "a great thing" for the firm. They were somewhat fearful of it at first, but now they are very glad they did not interfere with it. Mr. Bergner, who by the way is Republican, says frankly that the new law benefits their business in many ways. Here are his words:


"When we used to have the accounts and collections of ten saloons to look after now we have only one. That is, we have one risk and one customer. It simplifies our bookkeeping; but to our remaining customers we sell, strange to say, twice as much beer as we sold to the raft of customers we had before the high license went into force. Altogether we are very well satisfied with this new state of affairs, for under the old system we were continually on the anxious bench about dozens of shaky customers. Now, about all of them are responsible men, with large and growing interests."


The Wholesale dealers in liquors and wines say there has been a falling off in their trade since the high license law came into effect; but they do not attribute this entirely to the operation of the law, since the consumption of their goods always becomes less in summer. Even if the law did materially diminish this branch of the business, that is more than balanced by the increase in the beer trade. It is strange that the Brooks Law, which was expected to be a great blow for the brewing interest and a benefit to the distillers, has resulted just the other way. Like all other permissive measures, the Pennsylvania law has failed in the part essential to the interests of Society. The trade in alcoholic drinks flourishes and grows great under its protection, and any apparent merit it possesses is outweighed a hundred fold by the injury wrought by its agency.

It would be a good investment at that figure, even as things are, and besides, I should like to have that place. Twenty-five thousand, only twenty thousand, and now when I want it I have not got it. And should have had it if it had not been for that tiger, that devil Edith. She has had more than that out of me in the last ten years, and still she is threatening and crying for more, more, more. Tiger—yes, that is the name for her; her own name, too. She would coin one's vitals into money if she could. All Belle's fortune she has had, or nearly all, and most of my savings, and now she wants another five hundred, and she will have it, too. Here we are" and he drew a letter from his pocket written in a bold but somewhat uneducated woman's hand.

"Dear Bill" it ran—"I've been unlucky again and dropped a pot. Shall want £500 by the 1st October. No shuffling, mind; money down; but think that you know me too well to play any more larks—When can you tear yourself from the lovely Mrs. E., and come and give your E. a look? Bring some tin when you come, and we will have times. Thine, THE TIGER."

"The Tiger, yes, the Tiger" he gasped, his face working with passion and his gray eyes glinting as he tore the epistle to fragments, and threw them down and stamped on them.

"Well, be careful that you don't one day cut your claws and paint your stripes. By heaven! I never a man felt like murder so now. Five hundred more, and haven't five thousand clear in the world. Truly we pay for the follies of our youth! It makes me mad to think of those fools Cossey & Son forcing that place into the market just now. There's a fortune in it at the price. In another year or two I might have recovered myself, that devil of a woman might be dead, and have several irons in the fire, some of which would be sure to turn up trumps. Surely there must be a way out of it somehow. There's a way out of everything except death. If only one thinks enough, but the thing is to find it," and he stopped in his walk opposite to the window that looked upon the street and put his hand to his head.

As he did so he caught sight of the figure of a tall gentleman strolling idly toward the office door. For a moment he stared at him blankly, as a man does when he is trying to catch the vague clue to a new idea. Then, as the figure passed out of his view, he brought his fist down heavily upon the sill.

"Edward Cossey, by George!" he said, aloud. "There's the way of it, if only I can work him, and unless I have made a strange mistake I think I know the way."

A couple of minutes afterward a tall, shapely young man of about twenty-four or five years of age, came strolling into the office where Mr. Quest was sitting, to all appearance hard at work at his correspondence. He was dark in complexion and decidedly distinguished looking in feature, with large, dark eyes, dark mustaches and pale, somewhat Spanish looking skin. Young as the face was, it had, if observed closely, somewhat a worn and worried air, such as one would scarcely expect to see upon the countenance of a gentleman born to such brilliant fortunes, and so well fitted by nature to do them justice, as was Mr. Edward Cossey. For it is not every young man with dark eyes and good figure who is destined to be the future head of one of the most wealthy private banks in England, and to inherit in due course a sum of money in hard cash variously estimated at from half a million to a million sterling. Such, however, was the prospect of life that opened out before Mr. Edward Cossey, who was now supposed by his old and eminently business like father to be in process of acquiring sound knowledge of the provincial affairs of their house by attending to the working of their country branches in the eastern counties.

"How do you do, Quest?" said Edward Cossey, nodding somewhat coldly to the lawyer and sitting down. "Any business?"

"Well, yes, Mr. Cossey," answered the lawyer, rising respectfully, "there is some business, some very serious business."

"Good" said Ivy, "what is it?"

"Well, it is this: the house has ordered foreclosure on the Honham castle estates—at least it comes to that."

At the sound of this intelligence Edward Cossey's whole demeanor underwent the most startling transformation—his languor vanished, his eyes frightened, and his form became instinct with active life and beauty.

"What the deuce!" he said, and then paused. "I won't have it," he went on, jumping up. "I won't have it! I am not particularly fond of old De la Molle, perhaps because he is not particularly fond of me," he added, rather drolly; "but it would be an internal sham, to break up that family and sell the house from under them. Why, they would be ruined! And then there's Ida—Miss de la Molle, I mean—what would become of her? And in an old place, too. After being in the family for all these centuries, I suppose it would be sold to some confounded country skipper or some retired thief of a lawyer. It must be prevented at any price—do you hear, Quest?" The lawyer winced a little at his chief's contemptuous allusion, and then remarked with a smile: "I had no idea that you were so sentimental, Mr. Cossey, or that you took such a lively interest in Miss de la Molle," and he glanced up to observe the effect of his shot. Edward Cossey colored. "I did not mean that I took any particular interest in Miss de la Molle," he said; "I was referring to the family."

"Oh, quite so, though I am sure I don't know why you shouldn't. Miss de la Molle is one of the most charming women that I ever met, I think the most charming, if except my own wife Belle," and he again looked up suddenly at Edward Cossey, who, for his part, colored for the second time. Ellis, the slick young Young Men's

Oh what time it was! The hills Jared
under the rumbling of Gods chariots. Blind-
ing sheets of rain drove the cattle to the bars,
or beat against the window pane as though to
dash it in. The grain fields threw their
crowns OF gold at the feet of the storm king.
When night came in it was double night.
Its mantle was torn with the lightnings, and
into its locks were twisted the leaves of up-
rooted oaks and shreds of canvas torn from
the masts of the beached shipping. It was
such night as makes you thank God for
shelter, and open the door to let in the storm
bowling outside with terror.
We went to sleep under the full blast of
heavens great orchestra, the forests with up-
lifted voices in chorus that filled the moun-
tains, praising the Lord. We woke not until
the fingers of the sunny morn touched our
eyelids. We looked out the window and the
Housatonic slept as quiet as an infants
dream. Pillars of clouds set against the sky
looked like the castles of the blest built for
hierarchs on the beach of the azure
sea. All the trees sparkled as though there
had been some great grief in heaven, and
each leaf had been God-appointed to catch an
angels tear. It seemed as if our father had
looked upon the earth, His hayward child,
and stopped to her tear-wet cheek and kissed
it; so will the darkness Of sin and crime
leave our world before the dawn of the morn-

strike the forests of Maine and the masts Of
Mobile, and all between. And one end rest-
ing on the Atlantic coast and the other on the
Pacific beach. God will spring a great rainbow
arch to token that the world shall never more see
a deluge of crime.
But" says some one, "preaching against
the evils of society will accomplish nothing.
Do you not see that the evils go right on?" I
answer, we are not at all discouraged.
It seemed insignificant for Moses to stretch
his hand over the Red Sea—what power
could that have over the waters. But the
East wind blew all night; the waters gathered
into two glittering palisades on either
side. The pillows reared as Gods hand pulled
back upon their crystal bits. Wheel into line,
Israel! March, March! Pearls crash in!

the beach answers the shout of hosts mid-sea;

attained the beach, the shields clang, and the

stretch out the hand of prayer and Christian
fort over these dark, boiling waters of crime

heavens cymbals; while those who resist and

and there will be nothing left of them but
here and there, cast high and dry upon the
beach, the splintered wheel of the chariot
and thrust out from the surf, the breathless
postil of a riderless charger.
